The winter I turned fifteen, forty feet of the wall above my aunt Maren's top field lay in the grass. The Pellows, who farmed the place before her father, had built it with a through-stone every yard. What caused the collapse was her own tractor. Backing a trailer of hay in the November dark, she caught the end of the wall, and the whole run went down behind it like a shelf of books.

Dell Haskett drove up from the fencing yard in Orley with wire in his truck and a cost lower than her feed bill, and I was on his side before he finished. His fence would go up in two days, it would hold Maren's ram, and it would stand well back from the stream. Maren listened, then walked him to the gate, where a post he had set for the Dunmores two winters before leaned a hand's width out of the frost-hard ground. She said she would think about her choice. I thought she was being sentimental about a heap of rocks.

So I joined her every Saturday, grudgingly, catching each stone she sent across the gap with a short underhand pitch. It lasted about a month. Somewhere between learning to set a through-stone and learning to pack the hearting, I began to see the wall as she did: a thing that would outlast us both, built from what the field had already given.

In March the gap was one capstone short. Maren set the last one and kept her hand on it, looking down at the empty lower field. "When I was your age there were forty ewes on that slope, and now there are eleven and one ram," she said. She stood there with her hand on the stone until the light was gone.

That hard winter put me on the other side of the argument for good. In April, riding the bus past the fence Haskett had put up along the Orley road, I counted three posts already leaning out of the thawed ground, and I found I preferred my aunt's wall to every yard of his wire.

In the spring of 1852 the commissioners of Wexcombe County hired Thaddeus Varne, a self-taught surveyor from the canal country, to fix the boundary of Sallow Marsh. Between the farmers' old sea wall and the open mud lay a mile of marsh, cut by a winding creek, fringed with samphire, and marked each spring by a line of dried reeds where the highest tides had stopped. For a generation the farmers and the reed-cutters had quarreled over its edge, and both sides accused each other of moving the oak posts that Amos Rudd, paid by the farmers, had set eighty years before. Half the posts had rotted to stumps, and the commissioners wanted to know whether Rudd's line was still true.

Measuring from the tower of Sallow church, Varne found each of Rudd's surviving posts standing in freshly turned earth at the marsh's edge, a few yards nearer the farms than the rotted stumps of the row, and the only path to them ran from the reed-cutters' landing. He drove his own stakes along the place where the samphire stopped growing.

In June the militia draft took his second chainman, and Jonah Pell, who had only carried the far end of the chain, had to learn the whole work. Varne taught him to plumb the staff, count the links aloud and sight from stake to stake, and by August Pell was running long lengths of the line alone while Varne checked his figures from the punt.

Pell set the stake at Gull Point, where the creek meets the main channel, and asked whether the iron stub beside it was one of Rudd's. Varne knelt and held it for a long while. "That is all that is left of the stake my father drove here, the spring before the river took him."

In October Varne's eyes failed him, and Pell finished the survey alone, carrying the line to the sea wall in the first frosts. The winter tides left every stake standing. The commissioners accepted the map in Pell's hand, with Varne's name above his own, and the farmers and reed-cutters went on quarreling as before.

passage:
When Ines Farrow cleared her great-aunt Odile’s attic in Carrow last spring, she found a flat tin canister wedged behind the chimney. Inside lay one reel of film; on the lid someone had pencilled “Fair Day, Ferry St.” Her older brother, Colm, who had inherited the house with her, took the canister from her hands, climbed back up the ladder and set it behind the chimney exactly where it had been.

Ines brought it down the next morning, and they argued about it all summer. At last she took it to Teodor Brask, who owns the Lantern on Ferry Street and keeps its piano as it was in the early years, and he telephoned Wren Halloway, an archivist in Dunmere. Mabel Quill, the Lantern’s old pianist, who has played for its silent nights since she was a girl, was at the piano, and after a few chords she said its pitch had sagged so far that it needed a tuner.

Halloway unwound a few feet in the lobby, and it was Brask who placed the scene. Holding a frame to the window, he matched the striped awning in one corner to the one still over the bakery across the road. It had been filmed from the Lantern’s roof, looking down on their own town.

The archivist found the reel sound and supple, and after a short delay the archive made a copy, for a fee Ines paid herself. A collector in the city offered to buy the original, and neither answered. Colm still argued that a family film belonged in the family’s house; Ines, that it belonged to the street it showed. In September Colm agreed to let the original go to the archive if the copy came home.

In October the copy was screened at the Lantern to a full house, and the reel showed the town exactly what the pencilled lid had promised. Afterward, Brask asked Mabel whether she would play for the next showing. She said she would, and told him that the last time she had played to a house that full, her sister, twenty years gone now, had been sitting in the third row.
